sentences.text: This creature possessed a short, blunt snout where the front part was roughly as long as the back of the head from the eye sockets.
Its skull was relatively deep, a condition paleontologists call altirostry.
The bottom of the skull contained a tiny opening near the nose and two small holes below the eyes that were smaller than the eye sockets themselves.
One preserved specimen reveals that the front upper jaw bones held five teeth each.
Teeth located toward the rear of the jaw were low-crowned and bulbous in shape.
Despite being a crocodilian, this animal remained small, reaching a maximum length of only 2 meters.
It sported at least two distinct types of bony armor, including square-shaped plates with a concave underside likely used for back protection.
Remains of this animal have been unearthed within the Krabi Basin located in southern Thailand.
French and Thai scientists led by Varavudh Suteethorn and Eric Buffetaut recovered the material between 1989 and 1994.
Paleontologists Jeremy A. Martin and Komsorn Lauprasert first named the genus in 2010.
The species K. siamogallicus serves as the type species for the genus.
Like other extinct alligatorines, Krabisuchus was probably more terrestrial than semiaquatic.
The land environment where it lived is generally interpreted as a closed, densely vegetated subtropical to tropical forest.
Evidence for this forested habitat includes the presence of diverse arboreal fauna such as colugos, primates, and flying foxes.
The presence of the fully terrestrial plant Magnolia champaca suggests that the forests of the Krabi Basin were terrestrial rather than mangrove swamps.
Researchers suggest that Krabisuchus used its blunt teeth to crack hard-shelled prey items, similar to other orientalosuchins.
The genus was originally classified as a member of the group Alligatoroidea.
A 2014 study by Skutschas and colleagues recovered Krabisuchus as a basal member of Alligatoridae in a polytomy with Allognathosuchus, Hassiacosuchus, Navajosuchus, and the Maoming alligator.
It is closely related to the extinct alligatorines Arambourgia, Allognathosuchus, and Procaimanoidea.
The parent group of Krabisuchus is Orientalosuchina.
Krabisuchus is known exclusively from Late Eocene sediments found in the Krabi Basin of southern Thailand.
The fossil-bearing sediments of the Krabi Basin consist of ancient river deposits, a primary coal seam, and overlying lake deposits.
This animal lived during the Eocene epoch.
The time range for Krabisuchus is from 37.71 to 33.9 million years ago.
The affinities of the clade Orientalosuchina are disputed.
Tobias Massonne and his team argued that features initially interpreted as sutures in Krabisuchus were actually pre-orbital ridges.
It is debated whether the placement of Krabisuchus within Alligatoroidea is supported by all phylogenetic studies.
It is debated whether a longirostrine crocodilian previously referred to Eosuchus should be classified in the genus Maomingosuchus rather than Krabisuchus.
